reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes buying Hashflare power as a reliable way to earn money online and directs viewers to register through a link. The speaker recommends a roughly $300 purchase, conditionally ties higher returns to a Bitcoin price rise, and pairs registration and partner URLs with a “200 satoshi every hour” claim. A confirmation-stage order is shown, while a site notice warns of a temporary BTC withdrawal-fee increase and possible processing delays.

I want to make the daily revenue to a good sum so that from this income you can also reinvest from the income and keep growing in it.

the returns in the script you will have an increase of returns

opening.argument: Judge the speaker's return discussion as a conditional market forecast, not a promise of income. He says a higher Bitcoin price is something he thinks will happen, and describes increased returns in terms of what would follow if coin prices rise. He also says the other coin's exchange rate has not risen much so far. Those qualifications matter: a recommendation made in anticipation of a price move does not establish that buyers are promised a fixed return, or that the anticipated move will occur.

citations.quote: I think we will see a high price of Bitcoin in the future.
Since the exchange rate has not gone up very much so far it's better to take SHA256 and start working with it.
if bitcoin will rise according to this and in this sh 2500, then the returns will increase

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites a desire for daily revenue and a roughly $300 purchase, but neither quote promises that revenue will materialize. Its account of higher returns also leaves out the speaker's condition: Bitcoin must rise. The registration link is promotional, yet a link alone does not turn an uncertain market prediction into a guaranteed payout.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Conditional price forecasts do not remove the video's sales pitch. The speaker calls the service reliable for earning money online, recommends buying power, and describes daily revenue that could be reinvested. The defense's quotes show uncertainty about coin prices; they do not make the paid mining purchase incidental to the message.

opening.argument: This is substantially a walkthrough of an account operation. The speaker introduces his own investment, says he will show how power is bought, compares mining options, then narrates choosing a payment method and confirming the order. The sampled purchase screen shows an order and confirmation controls, while a later dashboard shows the account's hashpower display. A viewer can learn what this particular purchase flow looks like without treating the speaker's enthusiasm as proof that the service will pay out.

citations.quote: I would like to tell you how I invested $ 500 in this project. And I would like to show you how power is bought.
so we choose the method of payment pay from the balance How much do you get? I confirm the position. Confirm.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited purchase amount and confirmation stage establish that a purchase is being demonstrated, not that viewers are shown a realized return. The opening's daily-revenue quote expresses a goal for reinvestment, whereas the on-screen order documents what is being bought. The registration invitation makes the presentation promotional, but it does not erase the step-by-step demonstration that occupies the discussion.

citations.quote: I want to make the daily revenue to a good sum so that from this income you can also reinvest from the income and keep growing in it.
if you liked this service, register for the link below

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The operational walkthrough is also the mechanism of the pitch: the speaker tells viewers which power to buy and ties that choice to growing revenue. An order screen can demonstrate a transaction, but it cannot substantiate the claimed earning potential. The invitation to register through the link reinforces that this is promotion of paid mining capacity, not merely neutral instruction.

opening.argument: The observed transaction has the shape of an ordinary purchase of a specified service: the speaker selects SHA-256 hashpower, states a price, chooses payment from his balance, and confirms. The order screen shows a quantity, total, terms checkbox and payment controls; the subsequent dashboard displays hashpower. The description contains registration and partner links, but it does not say users must recruit others, disclose credentials, or receive a guaranteed return. Those missing claims matter when deciding whether this purchase demonstration itself establishes deception. The material shows a paid service being promoted, not proof of what purchasers ultimately receive.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening is right that money and anticipated revenue are involved. But its cited $300 line identifies the proposed hashpower purchase, while the confirmation screen shows an ordinary order flow. Neither establishes a guaranteed return or a request for credentials. The separate “200 satoshi every hour” phrase appears beside a partner link; the supplied description does not explain it as a payout from this SHA-256 purchase.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A displayed order and hashpower balance do not establish that buying the capacity yields the promoted income. The speaker explicitly recommends purchasing a particular mix, calls the project reliable for earning money, and urges viewers to register through his link. A guaranteed rate, credential request or recruitment requirement is not necessary to recognize the paid-mining-returns promotion shown here.
